tier_note: landmark; the field calls it a "course correction" (SIOP TIP, n52). Table 3 extraction was partly garbled in the fetch; verify each value against the published PDF.
citation: Sackett, P. R., Zhang, C., Berry, C. M., & Lievens, F. (2022). Revisiting meta-analytic estimates of validity in personnel selection: Addressing systematic overcorrection for restriction of range. Journal of Applied Psychology, 107(11), 2040–2068.
publisher: American Psychological Association (accepted manuscript mirrored on gwern.net)
population: US and international civilian job samples pooled from prior meta-analyses; e.g. structured interviews k = 36 / N = 3,069 (McDaniel 1994) and k = 69 / N = 4,795 (Huffcutt 2014); job knowledge k = 59 / N = 3,965; biodata k = 49 / N = 20,564; work samples k = 54 / N = 10,469
effect: revised operational validities: structured interviews .42, job knowledge .40, empirically keyed biodata .38, work samples .33, cognitive ability .31, integrity .31, assessment centers .29, SJT (knowledge) .26, interests .24, unstructured interviews .19, conscientiousness .19, years of experience .07
summary: Re-estimates the validity of the main selection procedures after showing that prior meta-analyses applied range-restriction corrections derived from predictive studies to the concurrent studies that dominate the databases, which overcorrected. The authors recommend no range-restriction correction for concurrent studies; the revised estimates fall by .10–.20 but the rank order of the strong predictors largely holds, with structured interviews now first and cognitive ability well down the list. Each validity is paired with a Black–White d so that the validity–diversity trade-off is visible: cognitive ability d = .79, work samples .67, job knowledge .54, structured interviews .23, integrity .10.
why_it_mattered: Reset the field's numbers: after the 2022 re-estimation, structured interviews rather than cognitive tests lead the validity table, and every method's group difference sits beside its validity, so the trade-off is visible in one table.
key_facts: Structured interviews .42 (was .51 in Schmidt & Hunter 1998); job knowledge .40 (was .48); biodata .38 (was .35); work samples .33 (was .54); cognitive ability .31 (was .51); unstructured interviews .19 (was .38); years of job experience .07 (was .18)

Black–White d: cognitive ability .79; work samples .67; job knowledge .54; assessment centers .52; years of experience .49; SJT .39; biodata .33; interests .33; unstructured interviews .32; structured interviews .23; integrity .10; conscientiousness −.07
Recommendation: apply no range-restriction correction to concurrent (incumbent) validation studies; hiring-rate-based U ratios are unreliable
The d values mix applicant, incumbent and national samples and are offered to locate predictors as having large, modest or minimal group differences
quotes: we recommend no range restriction correction for concurrent studies
role_note: the current standard for what predicts job performance; anchors the select stage and the cognitive-ability controversy
anchor: Sackett, Zhang, Berry & Lievens (2022), Journal of Applied Psychology; revised validity estimates for selection methods

citation: Oh, I.-S., Le, H., & Roth, P. L. (2023). Revisiting Sackett et al.'s (2022) rationale behind their recommendation against correcting for range restriction in concurrent validation studies. Journal of Applied Psychology, 108(8), 1300–1310.
population: reanalysis of the conditions in Sackett et al. (2022) Tables 1 and 5
effect: argues range restriction in concurrent studies is larger than Sackett et al. assume; no new validity table
summary: The published rebuttal. Sackett et al. said range restriction in concurrent studies is small unless the selection variable correlates about .90 with the predictor and selection ratios are .30 or lower; Oh, Le and Roth argue both conditions are plausible, that Table 5 understates the bias, and that the no-correction recommendation lacks support. Sackett et al. replied in the same journal (not read; see todo).
key_facts: Disputes the two conditions (r ≈ .90 with the selection variable; selection ratio ≤ .30) Sackett et al. used to call concurrent range restriction negligible
Argues the Case IV correction in Sackett et al. Table 5 understates the severity of range restriction
role_note: one side of the cognitive-ability-validity controversy record

citation: Sackett, P. R., Zhang, C., Berry, C. M., & Lievens, F. (2023). Revisiting the design of selection systems in light of new findings regarding the validity of widely used predictors. Industrial and Organizational Psychology, 16(3), 283–300.
population: conceptual follow-up to Sackett et al. 2022
effect: no new estimates; recommendations on correcting for criterion unreliability and range restriction in applied work
summary: The practitioner-facing follow-up: what the revised estimates mean for the relative standing of predictors, for the validity–diversity trade-off, and for attending to the variability of validity estimates rather than their means. It summarises the reactions to the 2022 paper and gives recommendations for applied validity corrections. Only the abstract was read; the recommendations themselves are a todo.
key_facts: Argues for attending to the variability of meta-analytic validity estimates, not only the mean
Summarises reactions to Sackett et al. (2022) and offers recommendations for applied corrections
role_note: the authors' own guidance on using the revised estimates in a selection system

citation: Schmidt, F. L., & Hunter, J. E. (1998). The validity and utility of selection methods in personnel psychology: Practical and theoretical implications of 85 years of research findings. Psychological Bulletin, 124(2), 262–274.
publisher: American Psychological Association (PDF mirrored by a vendor site)
population: cumulative meta-analytic estimates across 85 years of selection research
effect: GMA .51; work samples .54; integrity .41; conscientiousness .31; structured interviews .51; unstructured interviews .38; job knowledge .48; years of experience .18; biodata .35; assessment centers .37; years of education .10; interests .10
summary: The paper every selection textbook cited for two decades: Table 1 gives the corrected validity of nineteen predictors and the gain each adds to general mental ability. It made GMA the focal predictor and named GMA plus integrity (R = .65), GMA plus work sample (.63) and GMA plus structured interview (.63) the best combinations. Sackett et al. (2022) revised most of these values downward; it is carried here as the baseline the revision is measured against.
key_facts: Validity alone: GMA .51; work sample .54; integrity .41; conscientiousness .31; structured interview .51; unstructured interview .38; job knowledge .48; job tryout .44; peer ratings .49; reference checks .26; years of experience .18; biodata .35; assessment centers .37; years of education .10; interests .10; graphology .02; age −.01
Best GMA-plus-one combinations: integrity test R = .65; work sample .63; structured interview .63
role_note: the pre-2022 baseline; needed to read the controversy record

citation: McDaniel, M. A., Whetzel, D. L., Schmidt, F. L., & Maurer, S. D. (1994). The validity of employment interviews: A comprehensive review and meta-analysis. Journal of Applied Psychology, 79(4), 599–616.
publisher: American Psychological Association (PDF mirrored by a university course site)
population: 245 validity coefficients, N = 86,311; job-performance subset k = 160, N = 25,244
effect: overall ρ .37; structured .44 (k = 106, N = 12,847) vs unstructured .33 (k = 39, N = 9,330); situational .50; job-related .39; psychological .29; individual .43 vs board .32
summary: The interview meta-analysis that established structure as the main moderator: structured interviews out-predict unstructured ones, situational questions out-predict job-related and psychological ones, and individual interviews out-predicted boards in this dataset. Validity was similar for job and training performance and lower for tenure. Sackett et al. (2022) re-use its structured-interview database without the range-restriction correction.
key_facts: Structured ρ .44 vs unstructured ρ .33 for job performance
Situational content ρ .50; job-related .39; psychological .29
Within structured interviews, individual ρ .46 vs board .38; the authors call several subgroup results tentative
role_note: the structure effect in its original form

citation: Levashina, J., Hartwell, C. J., Morgeson, F. P., & Campion, M. A. (2014). The structured employment interview: Narrative and quantitative review of the research literature. Personnel Psychology, 67(1), 241–293.
publisher: Wiley (abstract via Utah State University Digital Commons, which dates the online-first version 2013)
population: twenty years of structured-interview research since the Campion et al. structure frameworks
effect: narrative review with meta-analytic supplements; no single coefficient read
summary: Reviews eight topics in structured interviewing: defining structure, reducing bias, impression management, measuring personality, situational versus past-behaviour questions, rating scales, probing and follow-up, and reactions to structure, and closes with twelve propositions and nineteen research questions. Only the abstract was read; the component-level findings are a todo.
key_facts: Eight review topics; twelve propositions and nineteen research questions for future work
quotes: much is known about structured interviews
role_note: the component anatomy of a structured interview (what "structure" means in practice)

citation: Kuncel, N. R., Klieger, D. M., Connelly, B. S., & Ones, D. S. (2013). Mechanical versus clinical data combination in selection and admissions decisions: A meta-analysis. Journal of Applied Psychology, 98(6), 1060–1072.
publisher: American Psychological Association (PDF mirrored on gwern.net)
population: job performance: k = 9; N = 1,392 (mechanical) and 1,156 (clinical)
effect: job performance validity r = .44 for mechanical combination vs .28 for holistic/clinical combination of the same predictors
summary: When the same predictor information is combined by formula rather than by judgement, prediction of job performance improves by more than half (r .44 vs .28). The authors conclude that experts are good at collecting information and poor at combining it, and recommend mechanical screening, mechanical scores as the anchor for any adjustment, documented deviations, and averaging across raters. Values are probably underestimates because no range-restriction or unreliability corrections were possible.
why_it_mattered: Turned a judgement question into a measured one: combining the same information by formula beats combining it by feel by more than half, which is the evidence behind scored rubrics and documented overrides.
key_facts: Job performance: mechanical r = .44 (cross-validated .40) vs clinical r = .28; k = 9
Recommended practice: screen mechanically; use the mechanical score as the anchor; document deviations; average raters
quotes: consistent and substantial loss of validity when data were combined holistically
data combination is best done mechanically while information collection can be done quite effectively by experts
role_note: the evidence behind scored rubrics and against gut-feel overrides

citation: Dana, J., Dawes, R., & Peterson, N. (2013). Belief in the unstructured interview: The persistence of an illusion. Judgment and Decision Making, 8(5), 512–520.
publisher: Society for Judgment and Decision Making (open access)
population: three laboratory studies with student interviewers predicting students' GPA; Study 3 n = 169
effect: predictions made with an unstructured interview r = .31 vs .61 without one; prior GPA alone .65; 57% ranked a random interview above no interview
summary: Shows two mechanisms that keep the unstructured interview alive: sensemaking (interviewers form confident impressions even from random answers) and dilution (the interview degrades the use of valid information). Adding an interview halved predictive accuracy, interviewers could not tell random interviews from real ones, and most people still preferred a random interview to none. The authors conclude unstructured interviews should not be used for screening decisions.
key_facts: Study 1: predictions with interview r = .31; without r = .61; prior GPA alone r = .65
Interviewers given random answers rated their impressions as useful as those given accurate answers
Study 3: 96 of 169 (57%) ranked a random interview above no interview
role_note: why hiring teams keep trusting the method with the least validity

citation: Kausel, E. E., Culbertson, S. S., & Madrid, H. P. (2016). Overconfidence in personnel selection: When and why unstructured interview information can hurt hiring decisions. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 137, 27–44.
journal: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
population: Study 1: 132 hiring decision-makers; Study 2: 70 hiring decision-makers; Study 3: 149 undergraduates in a betting task
effect: accuracy with test scores only .69/.72/.66 vs with unstructured interview ratings added .62/.63/.61; overconfidence rose in every study; betting earnings 143.7 vs 90.8 points
summary: Hiring managers who saw general mental ability and conscientiousness scores alone predicted performance better than those who also saw unstructured interview ratings, and were less overconfident. The effect held when the number of predictors was equalised, so it is not an information-quantity artefact. In the betting study, the interview condition bet more, was more overconfident, and earned less.
key_facts: Study 1 (132 managers): accuracy .69 tests only vs .62 with interview; overconfidence ≈ .05 vs .16
Study 2 (70 managers): accuracy .72 vs .63 with equal predictor counts
Study 3 (149 students): earnings 143.71 vs 90.75 points; confidence largely unrelated to accuracy
role_note: the cost of adding an unstructured interview to a valid test

citation: Hoffman, M., Kahn, L. B., & Li, D. (2018). Discretion in hiring. Quarterly Journal of Economics, 133(2), 765–800. (NBER Working Paper 21709, 2015, revised 2017.)
publisher: National Bureau of Economic Research (working-paper page; journal version at Oxford University Press)
population: 15 firms employing low-skilled service-sector workers; staggered introduction of a job test
effect: managers who hired against the test's recommendation made worse hires on average; test scores identified longer-staying workers
summary: Uses the staggered rollout of a pre-employment test across fifteen service firms to ask whether managers who override the test have private information. On average they do not: hires made against the test recommendation were worse, so discretion mostly reflected bias or error. The abstract and NBER digest were read; the tenure and productivity point estimates are a todo.
key_facts: Managers exercising discretion against test recommendations ended up with worse average hires when applicant pools were similar
Pre-employment test scores better identified workers who would stay longer
role_note: field evidence that overriding a valid screen costs quality

citation: Autor, D. H., & Scarborough, D. (2008). Does job testing harm minority workers? Evidence from retail establishments. Quarterly Journal of Economics, 123(1), 219–277. (NBER Working Paper 10763, 2004.)
publisher: National Bureau of Economic Research (working-paper page; journal version at MIT Press)
population: a national retail firm whose 1,363 stores switched from informal to test-based screening within one year
effect: testing raised median tenure by more than 10 percent with no measurable change in minority hiring; gains were roughly uniform across groups
summary: A natural experiment on whether adding a standardised test trades equity for efficiency. Minorities scored lower on the test, yet testing did not reduce minority hiring, and the productivity gains (tenure up more than 10 percent) were spread evenly across groups. The authors read this as the test replacing an informal screen that was no less biased, so the test added precision without adding negative information about minority applicants.
key_facts: 1,363 stores; median tenure rose by more than 10 percent after testing
No measurable impact on minority hiring despite lower minority test scores
role_note: evidence that a standardised screen need not reduce minority hiring in practice; pairs with the validity–diversity trade-off

citation: Phillips, J. M. (1998). Effects of realistic job previews on multiple organizational outcomes: A meta-analysis. Academy of Management Journal, 41(6), 673–690.
publisher: Academy of Management (abstract via Penn State Pure)
population: 40 studies (26 published) of realistic job previews
effect: RJPs associated with higher performance, lower attrition during recruitment, lower initial expectations, and lower voluntary and total turnover; numeric effect sizes not read
summary: The first comprehensive RJP meta-analysis: forty studies across five outcomes. Previews lowered initial expectations and attrition from the recruiting process and reduced voluntary and total turnover, with timing, medium and lab-versus-field design as moderators. Only the abstract was read; the effect sizes are a todo.
key_facts: 40 studies; outcomes: attrition during recruitment, level and accuracy of expectations, affective reactions, performance, turnover
Timing and medium of the preview moderated the effects; methods should match the outcome targeted
role_note: the evidence behind surfacing hard facts early

citation: Earnest, D. R., Allen, D. G., & Landis, R. S. (2011). Mechanisms linking realistic job previews with turnover: A meta-analytic path analysis. Personnel Psychology, 64(4), 865–897.
publisher: Wiley (abstract via Warwick Research Archive Portal)
population: 52 studies, about 17,000 participants
effect: perceived organizational honesty is the primary mechanism linking RJPs to lower voluntary turnover; most effective RJPs may be oral or written and delivered after hiring
summary: Tests how previews reduce turnover and finds that the honesty signal, not met expectations or self-selection, carries the effect: people stay with employers they believe were straight with them. Moderators suggest oral or written previews delivered after hiring work best, which reframes the RJP as a trust-building act rather than only a screening device. Abstract read; the path coefficients are a todo.
key_facts: 52 studies, ~17,000 participants; organizational honesty identified as the primary mechanism
Most effective previews may be oral or written and delivered after hiring, designed to signal honesty
role_note: why candour about pay, site and clearance early is retention work, not only screening

citation: Hausknecht, J. P., Day, D. V., & Thomas, S. C. (2004). Applicant reactions to selection procedures: An updated model and meta-analysis. Personnel Psychology, 57(3), 639–683.
population: 86 independent samples, N = 48,750
effect: favourability (5-point): interviews 3.84, work samples 3.63, résumés 3.57, references 3.33, cognitive tests 3.14, personality 2.88, biodata 2.81, personal contacts 2.51, honesty tests 2.47, graphology 1.76; perceptions correlate with attraction, offer-acceptance and recommendation intentions (average r range .08–.52)
summary: How applicants see the process matters for whether they stay in it: positive perceptions of selection predict organisational attractiveness, intention to accept an offer and willingness to recommend the employer, while being almost unrelated to gender, age and ethnicity. Interviews and work samples are the best-liked procedures, cognitive tests sit in the middle, and personality, honesty tests, biodata and graphology are least liked. Face validity and perceived predictive validity drive the justice judgements.
why_it_mattered: Showed that applicants' view of the process predicts whether they stay in it and accept, and ranked the methods by how they are received, which is why interviews and work samples carry the selection stage.
key_facts: 86 samples, N = 48,750
Interviews (3.84) and work samples (3.63) rated most favourably; honesty tests (2.47) and graphology (1.76) least
Procedural justice to organisational attractiveness average r .15–.50 depending on timing
role_note: the applicant side of every selection choice; links procedure choice to withdrawal and acceptance

citation: Becker, W. J., Connolly, T., & Slaughter, J. E. (2010). The effect of job offer timing on offer acceptance, performance, and turnover. Personnel Psychology, 63(1), 223–241.
publisher: Wiley (abstract via University of Arizona Experts)
population: archival field data from one large company, N = 3,012 (906 student and 2,106 experienced candidates)
effect: earlier post-interview offers were more likely to be accepted in both groups; no difference in later performance ratings or turnover by offer speed
summary: The one field study of offer speed: in both student and experienced pools, faster offers after the interview were more often accepted, and the people hired on fast offers performed and stayed no differently from those hired on slow ones. The authors conclude employers can speed offers to lift acceptance and shorten vacancies without a quality penalty.
key_facts: N = 3,012 from one company; two candidate pools with different recruiting processes
No difference in performance ratings or turnover between fast-offer and slow-offer hires
quotes: job seekers of both types were more likely to accept earlier offers
role_note: the evidence behind decision speed and reserved approval ranges

citation: Ryan, A. M., Sacco, J. M., McFarland, L. A., & Kriska, S. D. (2000). Applicant self-selection: Correlates of withdrawal from a multiple hurdle process. Journal of Applied Psychology, 85(2), 163–179.
population: 3,550 police applicants in a multiple-hurdle process
effect: applicants who withdrew differed from those who stayed on perceptions of the organisation, career commitment, job expectations, employment status, relocation, views of family and friends, and perceptions of the hiring process; early and late withdrawers differed; African American and female applicants held different perceptions
summary: The study of who drops out of a long multi-stage process and why. Withdrawal tracked perceptions of the organisation and the process, career commitment, current employment, the need to relocate and the views of family and friends; the reasons differed by stage, and minority and female applicants saw the process differently from the majority group. Abstract read; withdrawal rates and effect sizes are a todo.
key_facts: N = 3,550; withdrawal correlates measured across hurdles
Early-stage and late-stage withdrawers differed; demographic groups differed in perceptions
role_note: the only large field study of mid-process withdrawal found in this sweep

citation: Quality Improvement Center for Workforce Development (QIC-WD). Umbrella summary: Work sample tests. October 2021. Cites Roth, Bobko & McFarland (2005), Personnel Psychology, 58, 1009–1037.
population: summary of meta-analytic evidence for public child-welfare agencies
effect: work samples are relatively strong predictors for people who already hold the required KSAs; no coefficient given
summary: A government-funded evidence summary that carries the Roth, Bobko and McFarland (2005) work-sample meta-analysis and the practical conditions: build the test from a job analysis, standardise administration and scoring, use it for prerequisites that will not be trained, and get expert help because development is technically demanding. Used here as a pointer to the primary meta-analysis, which was not read (todo).
key_facts: Recommends job-analysis-based design, standardised administration and scoring, and expert consultation
Lists Roth, Bobko, McFarland & Buster (2008) on Black–White differences in work sample scores (not read)
role_note: pointer to the work-sample primary literature and its practical conditions

citation: Roth, P. L., Van Iddekinge, C. H., Huffcutt, A. I., Eidson, C. E., & Bobko, P. (2002). Corrections for range restriction in structured interview ethnic group differences: The values may be larger than researchers thought. Journal of Applied Psychology, 87(2), 369–376.
publisher: American Psychological Association (abstract via University of Iowa repository)
population: two forms of a behavioural interview used as an initial screen
effect: corrected Black–White d of .36 and .56, larger than the small differences earlier studies reported
summary: A caution on the claim that structured interviews have small ethnic group differences: once range restriction from using the interview as an initial screen is corrected, the two behavioural interview forms studied show d of .36 and .56. Sackett et al. (2022) carry .23 for structured interviews; this paper is why that figure is quoted with its caveat.
key_facts: Corrected d = .36 and .56 for two behavioural interview forms
quotes: substantially larger than previously thought
role_note: qualifies the "structured interviews have little adverse impact" claim

citation: Roulin, N., Bourdage, J. S., & Wingate, T. G. (2019). Who is conducting "better" employment interviews? Antecedents of structured interview components use. Personnel Assessment and Decisions, 5(1), Article 2.
population: 131 professional interviewers
effect: formal interviewer training and a selection (not recruitment) focus predicted use of question sophistication, consistency, note-taking and standardised evaluation; extraversion predicted rapport-building and probing
summary: Asks why interviewers who know structure works still resist it. Training and whether the interview is meant to select or to sell the job predicted the use of the structure components that carry validity; personality predicted the unstructured habits. The authors conclude formal training matters and that removing rapport and probing outright will meet resistance.
key_facts: N = 131 interviewers; seven structure components examined
Training is the modifiable antecedent of structured practice
role_note: why interviewer training is the lever, and why structure is resisted

citation: Rynes, S. L., Colbert, A. E., & Brown, K. G. (2002). HR professionals' beliefs about effective human resource practices: Correspondence between research and practice. Human Resource Management, 41(2), 149–174.
publisher: Wiley (abstract via University of Iowa repository, which lists the authors as Colbert, Brown & Rynes)
population: 5,000 HR professionals surveyed; 959 responded
effect: large research–practice gaps, largest in selection: practitioners place far less faith in intelligence and personality tests than the research supports
summary: The research–practice gap measured directly: nearly a thousand HR professionals were asked whether they agreed with established findings, and the biggest disagreements were about selection, especially the predictive power of intelligence and personality tests. Agreement was higher among senior, certified and literature-reading practitioners. Later replications (Fisher et al.; the "selection myths" studies) are not yet read.
key_facts: 959 of 5,000 HR professionals responded
Higher-level, SPHR-certified and academic-literature-reading practitioners agreed with research more often
role_note: why evidence-based selection is not the default in practice

citation: Behroozi, M., Shirolkar, S., Barik, T., & Parnin, C. (2020). Does stress impact technical interview performance? Proceedings of the ACM Joint European Software Engineering Conference and Symposium on the Foundations of Software Engineering (ESEC/FSE 2020). Reported in NC State University News, July 2020.
publisher: North Carolina State University (news release describing the peer-reviewed paper)
population: 48 computer-science students randomised to a watched whiteboard interview or a private room
effect: performance reduced by more than half when watched; stress and cognitive load higher in the traditional format; all women in the public condition failed and all in the private condition passed (sample too small for inference)
summary: A randomised trial of the whiteboard coding interview: being watched and asked to narrate halved performance on the same problem and raised measured stress. The authors argue the format confounds problem-solving with performance anxiety and propose private focus sessions with retrospective think-aloud. The news release was read; the paper's tables are a todo.
key_facts: n = 48; randomised; accuracy and efficiency scored
Proposed alternatives: private focus sessions, retrospective think-aloud
quotes: reduced by more than half, by simply being watched by an interviewer
role_note: the only experimental evidence found on the technical-interview format used by software firms

citation: Behroozi, M., Shirolkar, S., Barik, T., & Parnin, C. (2019). Hiring is broken: What do developers say about technical interviews? IEEE Symposium on Visual Languages and Human-Centric Computing (VL/HCC), 1–9.
publisher: IEEE (abstract via NSF Public Access Repository; NSF award 1755762)
population: qualitative analysis of Hacker News discussions among software practitioners
effect: recurring complaints: limited real-world relevance, bias toward younger developers, heavy time demands, anxiety and frustration, unwritten norms
summary: What developers themselves say about live-coding interviews, read off a large practitioner forum: the format feels unrelated to real work, favours the young and the recently drilled, takes a lot of time, and causes anxiety. The authors propose more inclusive formats such as collaborative problem-solving. Post counts were not in the abstract.
key_facts: Data: Hacker News discussions, qualitatively coded
Recommendation: collaborative problem-solving sessions and other inclusive formats
role_note: the candidate-side account of technical interviews, for the withdrawal and time-cost constraints

citation: Campion, E. D., Campion, M. A., Johnson, J., Carretta, T. R., Romay, S., Dirr, B., Deregla, A., & Mouton, A. (2024). Using natural language processing to increase prediction and reduce subgroup differences in personnel selection decisions. Journal of Applied Psychology, 109(3), 307–338.
publisher: American Psychological Association (author copy via Purdue)
population: four samples, N = 1,828, US Air Force Officer Training School selection
effect: NLP scores of narrative application text combined with tests and numeric data predicted board scores at r ≈ .60 (comparable to inter-rater agreement), added incremental validity, and reduced minority–nonminority subgroup differences in board scores
summary: Evidence that an algorithmic screen can be built to reduce adverse impact rather than add it: scoring applicants' narrative text with NLP predicted selection-board scores and training performance beyond tests and numeric data while narrowing racial subgroup differences. Relevant to the AI-screening gate as the kind of validation the regulations now expect.
key_facts: N = 1,828 across four samples; NLP + tests + numeric data r ≈ .60 with board scores
Subgroup differences in board scores reduced; incremental prediction of training performance
quotes: shows promise in addressing the validity-adverse impact dilemma in selection
role_note: what a validated algorithmic screen looks like

citation: Roth, P. L., Le, H., Oh, I.-S., Van Iddekinge, C. H., Buster, M. A., Robbins, S. B., & Campion, M. A. (2014). Differential validity for cognitive ability tests in employment and educational settings: Not much more than range restriction? Journal of Applied Psychology, 99(1), 1–20.
publisher: American Psychological Association (author copy via Purdue)
population: four simulation and reanalysis studies of Black and White subgroup validities
effect: apparent differential validity of cognitive tests by subgroup is largely an artefact of differential range restriction
summary: Addresses whether cognitive tests predict differently for Black and White applicants and concludes the apparent differences are mostly produced by range restriction that is stronger in Black applicant samples. Carried as background to the cognitive-ability controversy; the core of the record is Sackett et al. (2022) and the Oh et al. (2023) rebuttal.
key_facts: Common cutoffs restrict Black applicant variance more than White; common-ratio corrections can create illusory differential validity
quotes: the concept of differential validity may be largely artifactual
role_note: technical context for the subgroup-difference figures

citation: De Soete, B., Lievens, F., & Druart, C. (2013). Strategies for dealing with the diversity-validity dilemma in personnel selection: Where are we and where should we go? Journal of Work and Organizational Psychology, 29(1), 3–12.
journal: Journal of Work and Organizational Psychology
publisher: Colegio Oficial de Psicólogos de Madrid (open access)
population: narrative review of six strategy families, building on Ployhart & Holtz (2008)
effect: most promising: simulation-based assessments, alternative cognitive measures, statistical (Pareto-optimal) weighting; banding controversial; coaching gives small gains
summary: Reviews what can be done about the fact that the most valid tests show the largest ethnic score gaps. Simulations with low cognitive load and high fidelity, alternative cognitive measures and Pareto-optimal predictor weighting look most promising; reducing criterion-irrelevant variance, improving reactions and coaching help less; banding mainly works when minority preference is used within bands. The authors' summary is that there is no easy way out of the dilemma.
key_facts: Six strategy families reviewed; three judged most promising
Ployhart & Holtz (2008) credited for simulations and for the banding finding
quotes: there does not seem to be an easy way to tackle the diversity-validity quandary
role_note: the menu of adverse-impact strategies and their evidence

citation: Ployhart, R. E., Schmitt, N., & Tippins, N. T. (2017). Solving the Supreme Problem: 100 years of selection and recruitment at the Journal of Applied Psychology. Journal of Applied Psychology, 102(3), 291–304.
population: century review of selection and recruitment research in one journal
effect: no estimates; historical review with supplemental list of seminal articles
summary: The centenary review that frames selection and recruitment as applied psychology's "Supreme Problem" since 1917 and traces how business, legal and societal change moved the research. Carried as orientation; its supplemental seminal-article list is a snowball source for later sweeps.
key_facts: Supplemental material lists seminal articles and a timeline
role_note: orientation and snowball source

citation: Sackett, P. R., & Lievens, F. (2008). Personnel selection. Annual Review of Psychology, 59, 419–450.
population: review organised around eleven bases for improving selection
effect: no estimates
summary: The standard Annual Review of the field, organised around eleven routes to better selection: criteria, predictors, moderators, meta-analytic synthesis, new outcomes, accuracy, subgroup differences and fairness, administrative ease, applicant reactions and decision-maker acceptance. Abstract read; used for vocabulary and structure.

citation: Burks, S. V., Cowgill, B., Hoffman, M., & Housman, M. (2013). You'd be perfect for this: Understanding the value of hiring through referrals. IZA Discussion Paper 7382. Published as "The value of hiring through employee referrals", Quarterly Journal of Economics, 130(2), 805–839 (2015).

key_facts: 41–60 days to fill a cleared IT role (2021 survey)

population: 13,177 cleared professionals, late 2024
effect: average total compensation \$119,131 (up nearly 4%); DoD averages by level: Confidential \$90,834, Secret \$100,296, Top Secret \$124,084, TS/SCI \$132,177; full-scope polygraph \$141,299; contractors \$122,249 vs government \$115,348; 13% switched employers for pay in the past year; 40% at least somewhat likely to leave the cleared industry within five years

citation: Cullen, Z., & Pakzad-Hurson, B. (2023). Equilibrium effects of pay transparency. Econometrica, 91(3), 765–802. (NBER Working Paper 28903, 2021, revised 2022.)
publisher: National Bureau of Economic Research (working-paper page)
population: US private-sector workers under state laws protecting the right to ask about coworkers' pay
effect: right-to-discuss laws lowered wages by about 2% overall; effects muted where workers have little individual bargaining power (collective bargaining; posted wages)
summary: A bargaining model and a test: when workers can learn what coworkers earn, employers credibly refuse to pay any one worker more to avoid renegotiating with everyone, and average wages fall about two percent. The mechanism is strongest where pay is individually bargained, which is the small-firm case (synthesis). Abstract read; dispersion results and data are a todo.
key_facts: Wages ≈ 2% lower under state right-to-discuss laws
Mechanism: transparency shifts bargaining power to employers who avoid costly renegotiation
quotes: the laws lead wages to decline by approximately 2% overall
role_note: one side of the pay-transparency controversy; the compression mechanism behind internal equity

citation: Cullen, Z. (2024). Is pay transparency good? Journal of Economic Perspectives, 38(1), 153–180. (NBER Working Paper 31060.)
publisher: National Bureau of Economic Research (working-paper page)
population: review of transparency policies in 71% of OECD countries
effect: cross-worker transparency shrinks coworker pay gaps but lowers average wages through harder bargaining; vertical transparency raises motivation via accurate beliefs about earning potential; cross-firm transparency moves workers to higher-paying firms and intensifies wage competition
summary: The taxonomy that makes the transparency evidence legible: pay disclosure among coworkers, across seniority, and across firms do different things. Posting a range is cross-firm transparency, which pushes workers toward better-paying employers and sharpens competition; letting coworkers compare is cross-worker transparency, which compresses and lowers wages. Abstract read.
key_facts: Three types: cross-worker, vertical, cross-firm; effects differ by type
role_note: the frame for the pay-transparency controversy record

citation: Card, D., Mas, A., Moretti, E., & Saez, E. (2012). Inequality at work: The effect of peer salaries on job satisfaction. American Economic Review, 102(6), 2981–3003. (NBER Working Paper 16396.)
publisher: National Bureau of Economic Research (working-paper page)
population: University of California employees randomly informed of a public salary database
effect: below-median earners in their unit reported lower pay and job satisfaction and were significantly more likely to look for a new job; above-median earners reported no higher satisfaction
summary: The experiment on what happens when people learn what peers earn: those paid below their unit's median became less satisfied and more likely to search, and those above gained nothing. Satisfaction depends on relative pay and the response is asymmetric, which is the mechanism behind pay compression when a new hire comes in above incumbents (synthesis). Magnitudes are a todo.
why_it_mattered: The experiment that showed pay satisfaction is relative: told where they stood, below-median earners searched more and above-median earners gained nothing, the mechanism behind compression and the posted range.
key_facts: Information doubled use of the salary website; most looked up own-department colleagues
Asymmetric response: below-median lose satisfaction and search more; above-median unchanged
role_note: the relative-pay mechanism behind internal equity

citation: Bidwell, M. (2011). Paying more to get less: The effects of external hiring versus internal mobility. Administrative Science Quarterly, 56(3), 369–407.
publisher: SAGE (abstract via University of Pennsylvania ScholarlyCommons)
population: personnel records of the US investment-banking arm of a financial-services firm, 2003–2009
effect: external hires started about 18% higher than workers promoted into similar jobs; promoted workers significantly outperformed external hires for two years and had lower voluntary and involuntary exit; external hires were promoted faster
summary: The paper behind "paying more to get less": external hires into comparable jobs cost about eighteen percent more, performed worse for two years and left more often, while showing stronger visible credentials. It is the quantitative case for the internal-equity problem a market-rate offer creates, and for internal mobility as the cheaper route (synthesis).
why_it_mattered: Put a number on paying more to get less: external hires cost about eighteen percent more and performed worse for two years, the quantitative case for the internal-equity review before an offer.
key_facts: External hires paid ≈ 18% more than internal promotees into similar jobs
Promoted workers outperform external hires for the first two years; lower exit rates
role_note: the cost of external hiring to incumbents and to performance

citation: Maestas, N., Mullen, K. J., Powell, D., von Wachter, T., & Wenger, J. B. (2023). The value of working conditions in the United States and implications for the structure of wages. American Economic Review, 113(7), 2007–2047. (NBER Working Paper 25204.)
publisher: National Bureau of Economic Research (working-paper page)
population: stated-preference experiments with US workers, validated against actual job choices
effect: working conditions are a central part of compensation; willingness to pay for job characteristics varies by demographic group and across the wage distribution; accounting for it widens measured wage gaps
summary: The broadest estimate of what non-wage conditions are worth: a stated-preference design validated against real choices finds working conditions a central component of compensation with preferences that differ by group. The specific valuations (schedule flexibility, telework, paid leave, pace) were not in the abstract and are a todo; Mas and Pallais (n115) carry the two figures used in the records.
key_facts: Working conditions play a significant role in job choice; preferences differ by race, age, education and wage level
role_note: amenities as compensation

citation: Leibbrandt, A., & List, J. A. (2015). Do women avoid salary negotiations? Evidence from a large-scale natural field experiment. Management Science, 61(9), 2016–2024. (NBER Working Paper 18511.)
publisher: National Bureau of Economic Research (working-paper page)
population: nearly 2,500 job seekers randomly assigned to job ads with and without a statement that wages are negotiable
effect: without an explicit statement men negotiate more than women; when the ad says wages are negotiable the gender gap in negotiation disappears and tends to reverse; men prefer ambiguous wage rules; the gap is largest where negotiation is ambiguous
summary: A field experiment on one sentence in the ad: saying pay is negotiable removed the gender gap in who negotiates, while silence let it stand. For an offer process this is the cheapest equity lever found, and it interacts with the Equal Pay Act's rule that negotiation outcomes must still rest on job-related factors (synthesis).
key_facts: n ≈ 2,500; explicit negotiability statement closes or reverses the negotiation gap
role_note: the negotiability-statement lever

citation: Hansen, B., & McNichols, D. (2020). Information and the persistence of the gender wage gap: Early evidence from California's salary history ban. NBER Working Paper 27054, April 2020.
population: US workers in states with early salary-history bans; difference-in-differences and synthetic control
effect: the gender earnings ratio rose about 1% in states with bans, driven by recent job changers and workers over 35
summary: Early evidence on what the bans do: a one-percent rise in women's earnings relative to men's, concentrated among people who changed jobs, which is where an anchor on prior pay would have bitten. Working paper; later studies exist and are a todo.
key_facts: Gender earnings ratio +1% in ban states; effect driven by job changers
quotes: the gender earnings ratio increased by 1 percent in states with SHBs
role_note: what salary-history bans do to offers

citation: Arnold, D., Quach, S., & Taska, B. The impact of pay transparency in job postings on the labor market. NBER Working Paper 34480.
population: US states adopting pay-range posting laws; difference-in-differences across three datasets
effect: pay disclosure in postings rose about 30 percentage points; wages rose 1.3% to 3.6%; no effect on employment, posting volume, dispersion or skill requirements; gains attributed to increased competition with spillovers to incumbents and to firms that always posted pay
summary: The posting-law counterpart to the right-to-discuss result: requiring a range in the ad raised disclosure by thirty points and wages by one to four percent without reducing employment or postings, consistent with transparency across firms sharpening competition. Working paper; the Colorado detail and the applications result are a todo.
key_facts: Disclosure +≈30 pp; wages +1.3% to +3.6%; employment and postings unchanged
role_note: the other side of the pay-transparency controversy; the posting-range lever

citation: Federal Acquisition Regulation 16.601, Time-and-materials contracts. acquisition.gov.
population: contractors performing under time-and-materials or labor-hour contracts
effect: hourly rate defined as the contract rate for labor meeting the qualifications of a specified labor category; rates include wages, overhead, G&A and profit; separate rates per labor category for contractor, subcontractors and affiliates where not competitively awarded; ceiling price required; T&M only when the extent or duration of work cannot be estimated
summary: The contract type that fixes what a salary can be: each labor category has a fixed hourly rate that already contains the wage, the indirect costs and the profit, so the affordable salary is what remains after the firm's indirect rates and margin are subtracted (the "wrap rate" arithmetic, a synthesis). The rate applies only to labor that meets the category's qualifications.
why_it_mattered: The contract type that fixes what a salary can be: a labor category carries a fixed hourly rate containing wage, indirect costs and profit, so the offer stage starts from the rate, not the market.
key_facts: Hourly rate = rate for labor meeting the labor category qualifications; includes wages, overhead, G&A, profit (16.601(a), (b)(1))
Ceiling price required; D&F that no other type is suitable (16.601(d))
quotes: not possible at the time of placing the contract to estimate accurately the extent or duration of the work
role_note: the rate ceiling behind the affordable range

citation: Federal Acquisition Regulation 52.232-7, Payments under Time-and-Materials and Labor-Hour Contracts. Legal Information Institute.
population: contractors invoicing under T&M and labor-hour contracts
effect: labor hours for tasks with specified qualifications are not paid to the extent performed by employees who do not meet them, unless the contracting officer authorises; vouchers supported by records showing qualifications; 5% reserve up to \$50,000 possible
summary: The payment clause that turns a labor category's qualifications into a hiring constraint: hours worked by someone who does not meet the category's education or experience terms are not payable without the contracting officer's authorisation, and the firm must keep records that show qualifications. A candidate who can do the work but does not meet the category cannot be billed against it (synthesis).
key_facts: Hours by unqualified employees not payable absent CO authorisation (a)(3)
Vouchers supported by timekeeping and qualification records (a)(5)
quotes: will not be paid to the extent the work is performed by employees that do not meet the qualifications

citation: Federal Acquisition Regulation 31.205-6, Compensation for personal services. acquisition.gov.
population: contractors recovering compensation costs under cost-based contracts
effect: compensation allowable if reasonable for the work and conforming to an established plan; reasonableness judged against firms of similar size, industry and area doing similar non-government work; no presumption of allowability for major plan changes made without ACO review; bonuses allowable only under an agreement or plan established before the services; costs above the OFPP benchmark (41 U.S.C. 1127; all employees for awards on or after June 24, 2014) unallowable
summary: The cost principle that governs what a cost-type contractor can recover in pay: the salary must be reasonable by comparison with similar firms, a sign-on or retention bonus is allowable only under a plan that existed before the work, major compensation-plan changes need the administrative contracting officer's chance to review, and the all-employee cap applies. The cap rarely binds a small firm's technical hires but the plan and bonus rules bind every offer (synthesis).
key_facts: Reasonableness: comparison with firms of the same size, industry, geographic area and type of work (b)
Bonuses allowable only under a pre-existing agreement or plan (f); severance limited (g); pension supplements limited (j)
Cap: benchmark set by OFPP under 41 U.S.C. 1127; applies to all employees on awards from 2014-06-24 (p)(4); narrow exceptions for scientists and engineers possible
quotes: No presumption of allowability will exist
role_note: the allowability gate on offers and bonuses
